newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn forces D. Telekom to open network to rivals.
newsitem.headline: Bonn forces D. Telekom to open network to rivals.

text.p: The German government on Tuesday ordered phone giant Deutsche Telekom AG to grant rivals access to its local networks, a ruling that could prove to be crucial to ensuring competition in Europe's biggest telecoms market.

The ruling forces Deutsche Telekom to allow rivals to connect their networks directly to the telephone lines of businesses or residential customers without having to pay for any unwanted call switching services from Telekom.

By granting newcomers access to customers in the "last mile" of the telephone network, new companies hoping to compete against the incumbent monopoly will face lower costs and be able to price their services more competitively.

The ruling is more than symbolic as it could finally break a deadlock in competition in the "local loop" and it comes a day before Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet will choose the president of the new telecoms watchdog, the Regulatory Agency.

Post and Telecommunications Minister Wolfgang Boetsch, explaining the decision in an interview with Reuters, said the ruling was aimed at promoting competition and was visible evidence that Germany would exercise tough regulation.
"The last mile was always at the centre of the discussion," he said. "If the last mile cannot be bridged, or only with extraordinary costs, then competition will remain a theory."
"We have to prove that we are serious about regulation, otherwise companies with a dominant position in the market will press others up against the wall," he added.

Following complaints by rivals such as Mannesmann Arcor or the O.Tel.O. joint venture of utilities RWE AG and Veba AG, the ministry decided on May 28 that Telekom must offer rivals "unbundled interconnection".
But after Telekom failed to respond the ministry saw itself forced to issue a binding ruling and ordered Telekom to make such an offer by July 14 or face penalty proceedings.

Deutsche Telekom chairman Ron Sommer, speaking on the sidelines of a separate news conference in Bonn, compared such internconnection to "expropriation", but declined comment, saying he was not yet familiar with the ministry's decision.

"We want to consider this in peace and quiet and respond objectively," Sommer told reporters. Telekom later confirmed it had filed an appeal against the May 28 decision, which can not stop the new ruling from taking effect but forms the basis of an appeal in Administrative Court that could overturn it.
Germany and most European countries will allow full competition in telecommunications beginning on January 1, 1998.
A handful of international alliances have formed to offer competitive services from corporate communications and long-distance services to cable television and Internet access.
But the newcomers have patchy networks that do not reach into neighborhoods and city centres. Instead they still rent lines from Telekom in order to gain access to their customers.
The O.Tel.O consortium welcomed the government's ruling.
"The current confrontation with Telekom shows that we need a strong, competition-oriented regulator to open the telecommunications market," said O.Tel.O chairman Ulf Bohla.
Meanwhile, the government is set to appoint the president of the new telecoms Regulatory Agency on Wednesday.

It is widely expected to ignore a suggestion from the Regulatory Council, a temporary body made up of representatives from parliament and state government, to appoint Peter Landsberg, former Alcatel SEL chairman.
Boetsch is thought to support the appointment of Dieter Scheuerle, a senior post ministry official in charge of regulatory matters. He would not comment on the appointment.
Noting that full competition in European telecoms was just six months away, Boetsch acknowleged that more work needed to be done, but said the main reforms had been implemented.
"It is obvious that we won't be running at full throttle on January 1, 1998, but we are prepared. I am satisfied," he said.
